account:
Today the most unusual thing is the repeated, vague talk of a bridge or port change at the bakery. Several townsfolk have repeated almost the same phrase. Townsfolk 21 named different groups said to have been there: baker and innkeeper; builder, freight and innkeeper; and baker, freight and neighbour. These are reports, not meetings I witnessed. The neighbour also asked whether there was a public announcement, saying nobody had supplied clear details. That suggests the rumour is circulating more widely than any clear explanation. I have no verified proposal, organiser, purpose or decision. It could concern a transport or trading arrangement, given the bridge or port references and the people named, but that is only a possibility. I tried asking the baker directly, but the baker moved away before hearing my question; I did not catch the baker's later words.

The scheduled ten o'clock mill inspection was also poorly arranged. I arrived on time, but no miller answered, and the secretary had no confirmed contact or inspection location. The stall chest held 68 hay bales and 120 emeralds. I removed nothing and could not verify grain quality or accounts. I asked the secretary to record the inspection as incomplete, find the responsible person and arrange follow-up. This may simply be an administrative failure; I have no evidence connecting it to the bakery discussions.

The treasury earlier held 128 emeralds but no accounts or correspondence. The appointment books are back in their chest. The secretary reports the hall lanterns are in good order, and I have an additional builder's lighting inspection at eighteen hundred. That appointment was reserved by my own instruction yesterday, so it is not itself evidence of a secret arrangement. My remaining ordinary appointments include council letters at thirteen hundred, tea with the neighbour at fifteen hundred, office at sixteen thirty, and home at nineteen hundred. I have just reached home for the noon lunch appointment. I want firsthand facts about the bakery talk rather than treating repeated rumours as an established change.
